name: Facelift / neck lift

card.summary: Surgical lifting of the face and neck tissues; the most established anti-aging surgery, with decades of techniques and published complication data.
card.aka: rhytidectomy, deep plane facelift, SMAS lift, platysmaplasty
card.note: Hematoma and nerve injury are the main documented risks; reviews find no single technique clearly superior.

quick.overview:
A facelift (rhytidectomy) repositions and tightens facial tissues and usually removes excess skin to give a more youthful contour, and a neck lift addresses the jawline and neck, often by treating the platysma muscle. They are often combined.

In looksmaxxing forums, facelifts are discussed mainly as older-man anti-aging surgery and as a one-time investment, with arguments over whether to choose surgery or fillers. A review of facelift controversies concluded that the available techniques are generally equal in efficacy.
quick.mechanism: Techniques range from skin-only lifts to SMAS and deep plane lifts that reposition deeper layers, with neck work such as platysma plication or submental liposuction. Recent literature emphasises restoring volume and lifting vertically rather than pulling the skin sideways.
quick.risks: Documented complications include hematoma (the most common), nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring, hair loss at incisions and ear position changes. Wikipedia reports the ideal age for a facelift, by patient satisfaction, as 50 or younger, and cites typical skin-only results lasting 5 to 10 years.

lead: A facelift, or rhytidectomy, is cosmetic surgery intended to give the face a more youthful appearance, typically by removing excess skin, tightening deeper tissues and redraping the skin of the face and neck. It is commonly combined with eyelid surgery and neck procedures. [1]

Facelift techniques have evolved through cutaneous, SMAS, deep plane and volumetric periods since the early 1900s. [1] A review of facelift controversies concluded that the literature suggests available techniques are generally equal in efficacy and called for higher-quality research with standardised outcome assessment. [2]
In looksmaxxing communities, facelifts and mini neck lifts are discussed by older men and by people who have lost weight, usually as complements to jaw surgery or fat grafting. [3][4]
infobox: SMAS lift, deep plane, composite, MACS, mini-facelift
Third most popular aesthetic surgery in 2019 ASAPS data per Wikipedia [1]

paras: Wikipedia lists traditional, SMAS, deep plane, composite, mid-face, mini, subperiosteal, skin-only, thread-lift and MACS approaches. [1] Authors have described a lateral SMASectomy as a safe, reproducible technique producing results similar to a traditional SMAS flap without additional risk of nerve injury. [5]

For the neck, a vertical neck lifting approach is described as an extended deep plane facelift that redrapes laxity vertically onto the face, with indications for combining it with submental surgery. [6] A study of complete platysma transection examines platysma handling in neck rejuvenation. [7]
A review of male facelift notes that men seek a somewhat different outcome and that techniques have been adapted to preserve a masculine appearance. [8]

A review of facelift controversies found the options generally equal in efficacy. [2] A systematic review of patient-reported outcome measures covers facial cosmetic surgery and nonsurgical rejuvenation. [9] A Grokipedia summary reports a 2017 observer study in which patients looked about 3.7 years younger after facelifts. [10]

Wikipedia states a skin-only facelift can last 5 to 10 years, while Grokipedia gives longer durations for deep plane and composite lifts and about 1 to 2 years for thread lifts. [1][10] These longevity figures are secondary-source summaries.

Human evidence includes outcome-measure studies and large complication analyses. A pilot study tested instruments for measuring cosmetic facial plastic surgery outcomes in 78 patients, and an analysis of 11,300 patients examined preoperative risk factors and complication rates in facelift. [11][12]

Registered trials include a comparison of an office-based limited facelift with a hospital full facelift (n=100), a thread lift using retaining ligaments (n=369), and a study of intravenous tranexamic acid during rhytidectomy. [13][14][15] A non-surgical radiofrequency 'facelift' clinical study treated 20 areas in 17 patients. [16]

Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common complication, nerve injury (the greater auricular nerve for sensation, the facial nerve for motor function), skin necrosis with substantially higher risk in smokers, scarring, hair loss, ear position changes and rare infection. [1]
Grokipedia summarises hematoma at 2 to 5 percent and permanent nerve injury under 1 percent, and notes internal inconsistencies in its own figures. [10]

A looksmax.org post argues for saving about 15,000 dollars for a single limited facelift in a man's 40s or 50s, and says fillers can leave a face puffy; a reply disagreed that a facelift can only be done once and said results depend on the surgeon. [3]
Other members ask whether a neck lift before jaw surgery would address submental fullness, or whether a mini neck lift would help loose skin after weight loss. [4][17]

timeline.event: Eugen Hollander reportedly performs the first facelift in Berlin. [1]
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS. [1]
Start of the volumetric period of facelift surgery. [1]

lore.intro: Facelifts appear on looksmax.org in anti-aging threads and as add-ons for jaw and submental concerns. [3][4]

claims.claim: A facelift can only be done once or it looks odd
claims.believers: The original post says a limited facelift should be done once, in a man's 40s or 50s. [3]
claims.experts: A reply in the thread says facelifts can be repeated depending on the surgeon; the sources reviewed here do not address repeat facelifts. [3]

claims.claim: Surgery beats fillers for keeping a lean face
claims.believers: The post says fillers can make the face look puffy or bloated. [3]
claims.experts: Reviews describe facelift as repositioning tissue, and nonsurgical alternatives as a separate category; no head-to-head comparison is cited here. [1][2]

claims.claim: Jaw advancement surgery improves the submental area
claims.believers: A forum reply says maxillomandibular advancement stretches suprahyoid muscles and skin for a sharper submental area. [4]
claims.experts: The sources reviewed do not evaluate this.
